title: 4.7 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can solve real-world problems by using unit rates to compare options — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: A supermarket shelf tag shows two deals side by side for the same brand of juice boxes: a 6-pack for $3.00 and a 10-pack for $4.50. Neither tag says which pack is the better deal.
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: The Pizza Fundraiser
revealWordProblem.text: The 6th-grade class is buying pizza for a fundraiser. Pizza Palace sells 3 pizzas for $27.00, and Pizza Town sells 5 pizzas for $42.50. The class needs 15 pizzas. Which pizzeria should they order from, and how much will 15 pizzas cost at that price? Show your work.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Pizza Palace: $27.00 ÷ 3 = $9.00 per pizza. Pizza Town: $42.50 ÷ 5 = $8.50 per pizza. Since $8.50 is the lower unit rate, the class should order from Pizza Town. 15 pizzas × $8.50 = $127.50.

turnAndTalk.question: As supply manager you compare token deals like 500 for $60 and 350 for $38.50. You can't compare totals directly, so what does finding the cost 'per unit' let you do?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Finding the cost per one token lets me compare deals fairly even when the package sizes differ.

stems.en: I can't compare the totals because ___.
stems.es: No puedo comparar los totales porque ___.

stems.en: Finding the cost ___ lets me compare fairly.
stems.es: Hallar el costo ___ me deja comparar de forma justa.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain the packages have different quantities, so the per-unit cost (unit rate) is needed to compare deals fairly.
turnAndTalk.extend: Does the biggest package always have the lowest unit rate? Predict, then explain how you could be tricked by package size alone.
extendStems: The biggest package is not always cheapest per unit because ___.
Package size can trick you when ___.

turnAndTalk.question: How did the unit rate help you decide the better buy between the two token suppliers in your table?
turnAndTalk.kernel: I found the cost per token for each supplier and chose the lower one.

stems.en: The unit rate for ___ is $___ per token.
stems.es: La tasa unitaria de ___ es $___ por ficha.

stems.en: The better buy is ___ because its unit rate is ___.
stems.es: La mejor compra es ___ porque su tasa unitaria es ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students divide price by quantity for each deal (e.g., 350 for $38.50 = $0.11 each) and choose the supplier with the lower unit rate as the better buy.
turnAndTalk.extend: One supplier had the lower price per token but a higher total. Explain why a lower unit rate, not a lower total, is what makes a deal the better buy.
extendStems: A lower total does not mean a better buy because ___.
The unit rate is what matters because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Printer A makes 150 tickets in 5 minutes and Printer B makes 200 in 8 minutes. The manager needs 600 tickets fast. How do unit rates decide the faster printer and the time needed?
turnAndTalk.kernel: I find tickets per minute for each printer, pick the higher rate, then divide 600 by it.

stems.en: Printer A prints ___ tickets per minute and Printer B prints ___.
stems.es: La impresora A imprime ___ boletos por minuto y la B imprime ___.

stems.en: The manager should use Printer ___; 600 tickets take ___ minutes.
stems.es: El gerente debe usar la impresora ___; 600 boletos tardan ___ minutos.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students find 30 and 25 tickets/min, choose Printer A (higher rate), and divide 600 / 30 = 20 minutes.
turnAndTalk.extend: Here the higher unit rate is better, but for the token deals the LOWER unit rate was better. Explain why 'better' depends on what the rate measures.
extendStems: A higher rate is better when ___, but a lower rate is better when ___.
It depends on whether the rate measures ___ or ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Solve Problems with Unit Rates, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Divide the price by the number of items to get the cost per unit. The lower cost per unit is the better buy.

stems.en: The unit rate for ___ is $___ per token.
stems.es: La tasa unitaria de ___ es $___ por ficha.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.AT.2 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 4.7. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — How do I use unit rates to find the better buy?
conceptIntro.intro: A unit rate is the cost for just 1 item, like the price per token. When packages have different sizes, the unit rate lets you compare them fairly. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Divide the price by the number of items to get the cost per unit. The lower cost per unit is the better buy.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Fun Supply Co. sells 500 tokens for $60. I want the cost for 1 token.
I divide the price by the tokens: $60 ÷ 500 = $0.12.
So this deal is $0.12 per token. That is the unit rate.
Now I can compare it fairly to a deal with a different number of tokens.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Arcade Depot sells 350 tokens for $38.50. What do we divide?
What is the cost per token, and is it lower than $0.12? ($0.11 — yes, the better buy.)
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: Divide the price by the number of items to get the cost per unit. The lower cost per unit is the better buy..

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: Calculate the unit rate for each supplier's deal. Then determine which is the better buy for each item.

discourse.prompt: How do you use unit rates to determine the better buy?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I find the better buy by comparing the ___ for each option. The option with the ___ unit rate is the better buy because ___.

approaching.stem: Which is the better buy: 6 bouncy balls for $4.50 or 10 bouncy balls for $8.00?
choices: They cost the same per ball
choiceFeedback: Find the price per ball for each: divide cost by quantity.
Compare the unit prices.
Make sure you're dividing cost by quantity for each option.
hints: You can't compare $4.50 and $8.00 straight across — the packs hold different numbers of balls.
Find each pack's price for ONE ball (cost ÷ number of balls), then compare the two unit prices.
Start with the first deal: $4.50 ÷ 6. Then compute $8.00 ÷ 10 and see which per-ball price is lower.

approaching.stem: A faucet drips 15 ounces of water in 5 minutes. What is the unit rate?
choiceFeedback: Divide: 15 ounces ÷ 5 minutes.
Find the rate per minute.
Check: how much per one minute?
hints: The unit rate here is ounces per ONE minute — 15 ounces spread across 5 minutes.
Divide the ounces by the minutes so the time becomes 1 minute.
Set up 15 ÷ 5 ounces per minute.

approaching.stem: A printer prints 42 pages in 6 minutes. How many pages does it print in 15 minutes at the same rate?
approaching.explanation: Unit rate: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 pages per minute. In 15 minutes: 7 × 15 = 105 pages.
choiceFeedback: Divide: 42 pages ÷ 6 minutes.
Find the rate per minute.
Check: how many pages in one minute?
hints: This takes two steps: first find pages per ONE minute, then scale up to 15 minutes.
Divide to get the unit rate, then multiply that rate by the new time.
Step 1: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 pages each minute. Step 2: multiply that rate by 15 minutes.

approaching.stem: Store A sells 5 notebooks for $8. Store B sells 3 notebooks for $5.25. Which has the lower price per notebook?
approaching.explanation: Store A: $8 ÷ 5 = $1.60. Store B: $5.25 ÷ 3 = $1.75. $1.60 < $1.75, so Store A is cheaper per notebook.
choiceFeedback: Find the price per notebook for each store.
Compare the unit prices.
Which store has the lower price per notebook?
hints: Each store sells a different number of notebooks, so compare the price of ONE notebook at each store.
Divide cost by quantity for each store, then pick the smaller per-notebook price.
Store A: $8 ÷ 5 notebooks. Then compute Store B: $5.25 ÷ 3, and compare the two prices.

approaching.title: approaching — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Read
workedExample.work: Which gum deal is the better buy: 4 packs for $2.00 or 10 packs for $4.50?

workedExample.label: Attempt
workedExample.work: A student says: "$2.00 is less than $4.50, so 4 packs for $2.00 is the better buy."

workedExample.label: Check
workedExample.work: The student compared the total prices instead of the cost for one pack.

approaching.correctWork: Find the cost per pack first. 4 packs: $2.00 ÷ 4 = $0.50 per pack. 10 packs: $4.50 ÷ 10 = $0.45 per pack. Since $0.45 < $0.50, the 10-pack deal for $4.50 is actually the better buy.
hints: The packages hold different numbers of packs, so a smaller total price does not automatically win.
Divide each price by its number of packs, then compare those per-pack costs.

onLevel.stem: A machine dispenses 24 tokens in 3 minutes. At this rate, how many tokens does it dispense in 10 minutes?
onLevel.explanation: Unit rate: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 tokens per minute. In 10 minutes: 8 × 10 = 80 tokens.
choiceFeedback: First find tokens per minute: 24 ÷ 3. Then multiply by 12 minutes.
Find the unit rate, then use it to find the answer for 12 minutes.
You need to find how many tokens per minute first.
hints: Two steps: find tokens per ONE minute first, then stretch that rate to 10 minutes.
Divide tokens by minutes for the unit rate, then multiply the rate by the new time.
Step 1: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 tokens each minute. Step 2: multiply that rate by 10 minutes.

onLevel.stem: A factory produces 360 widgets in 8 hours. At the same rate, how many widgets are produced in a 12-hour shift?
onLevel.explanation: Unit rate: 360 ÷ 8 = 45 widgets per hour. In 12 hours: 45 × 12 = 540 widgets.
choiceFeedback: First find widgets per hour: 360 ÷ 8. Then multiply by 20 hours.
Find the unit rate, then use it to find the answer for 20 hours.
Start by finding how many widgets per hour.
hints: Two steps: find widgets per ONE hour first, then scale up to the 12-hour shift.
Divide widgets by hours for the unit rate, then multiply that rate by 12.
Step 1: 360 ÷ 8 = 45 widgets each hour. Step 2: multiply that rate by 12 hours.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Solve Problems with Unit Rates is comparing the total prices instead of the cost per item — the deal with the smaller total can still cost more per unit. Always reduce each option to its unit rate before you decide, then pick the lower one.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: A car travels 195 miles on 6 gallons of gas. What is the unit rate in miles per gallon?
choiceFeedback: Divide 195 miles by 6 gallons to find the unit rate.
The unit rate is miles per gallon.
Find: 195 ÷ 6 = ? miles per gallon.
hints: 'Miles per gallon' tells you the setup: miles on top, gallons on the bottom, for ONE gallon.
Divide the total miles by the total gallons — expect a decimal since 6 doesn't divide 195 evenly.
Set up 195 ÷ 6. (Check: 6 × 30 = 180, so the answer is a bit more than 30.)

smallGroup.label: Extra Support
smallGroup.who: Pull 3–5 students who struggled on the formative check / exit ticket for this lesson.
moves: Open with the worked example (I Do) — think aloud, don't just show.
Do the We Do together; require every student to say the sentence frame.
Release to the practice problems; the hint ladder is the safety net.

Watch for the common mistake: A common mistake in Solve Problems with Unit Rates is comparing the total prices instead of the cost per item — the deal with the smaller total can still cost more per unit. Always reduce each option to its unit rate before you decide, then pick the lower one.
Close with the exit-ticket check — celebrate the growth.
